title: Flying with a non-visible disability
lede: Aena has its own badge for people with non-visible disabilities. It is free, can be requested on its website and helps staff recognise that a person may need more time, understanding or support while moving through the airport.

p: As of 1 September 2026, Aena lists 20 airports where the badge can be used. Showing it gives access to the dedicated security lane for families and people with reduced mobility where the airport has one; if there is no dedicated lane, Aena states that, as far as possible, passage through the general security checkpoint will be facilitated.

The badge is not fast track, does not include an escort and does not exempt anyone from security checks or procedures. If travelling as a family, it is enough for one member to carry it. It can be shown in printed or digital form.

The Sin Barreras (PMR) assistance service is different. It is intended for people who need assistance while moving through the airport. It is advisable to request it in advance through the airline or Aena.

sections.h: A detail that is rarely explained
p: The sunflower lanyard is a private international initiative. Aena explains that it can indicate that a person needs more help or time, but it does not give access to the dedicated security lane. To receive Aena's specific provisions, the Aena badge must be requested.

Download the badge, check the airport map, locate quiet rooms if there are any, keep the boarding pass and documents together and set out the stages of the journey in writing beforehand. Aena provides support materials to help prepare for the route through the airport.

title: Public transport and getting around
lede: Getting around a city involves timetables, orientation, noise, crowds, platform changes, tickets and quick decisions. The barrier may lie in just one part of the journey rather than in ‘using public transport’ as a whole.

p: Prepare the route with a clear starting point and destination, save a screenshot of the journey, identify an alternative in case the service is cancelled and make sure there is enough battery power. For someone who needs it, a visual sequence of five or six steps may be more useful than a long explanation.

Accessible information, help locating a stop or platform, time to understand an instruction and reasonable access measures where there is a disability. Ley 15/2022 expressly includes transport among the areas protected against discrimination.

sections.h: If travelling alone is not yet safe
p: Practise one section at a time: first accompanied, then with agreed check-ins and finally independently if the person wants to and is able to. Autonomy does not mean withdrawing support too soon.

title: Shopping, errands and waiting
lede: Shopping brings together a list, money, decisions, travel, searching, lights, noise, interaction and changes when an item is unavailable. Separating those steps makes it easier to see what support is needed.

p: Use a short list arranged by area, keep the budget visible, take a photo of the item if the brand or format matters, and have a substitution plan: ‘if A is unavailable, I buy B; if B is unavailable too, I do not buy anything’.

Go at a quieter time, use self-checkout if it makes interaction easier, take headphones or glasses if they help, and split a large shop into two trips. Online shopping can be a functional support, not a ‘failure’ of autonomy.

Premises open to the public are subject to accessibility and non-discrimination obligations. A person can ask for information in a format they can understand and for reasonable and proportionate adjustments.

title: Restaurants and eating out
lede: Eating out adds smells, conversation, waiting, an unfamiliar menu, social expectations and less control over preparation. The difficulty is not simply a matter of ‘being selective’.

p: Look at the menu and photos, ask about ingredients or cross-contamination when clinically relevant, book a quiet table and choose a less busy time. If the person needs a safe food, check the venue's policy beforehand.
Ask for components separately, remove sauces or side dishes, request a simple explanation of the dish and allow the person to stop eating without turning it into a public negotiation.

Rules on goods and services require accessibility and non-discrimination for disabled people, but they do not require a restaurant to prepare any conceivable dish. The request needs to be specific and feasible; for allergies or coeliac disease, the relevant food-safety rules must also be followed.

title: Cinema, theatre and museums with fewer sensory demands
lede: Relaxed performances and low-stimulation visits reduce some barriers involving noise, lighting, waiting and rules about remaining in place. They are not only for autistic people: they may also be useful for hyperacusis, misophonia, anxiety, APD, sensory overload or other needs.

p: In Spain, some cinemas, theatres, museums and cultural centres schedule relaxed performances or lower-stimulation time slots. Common measures include keeping some lighting on, reducing volume, removing trailers or unnecessary effects, allowing people to enter and leave, and providing information about the space in advance.
Availability varies by city and programme, so it is advisable to check directly with the venue before travelling there.

Advance information about duration, lighting, sounds, queues and rules; a seat near an exit; the option to wait outside the queue; permission to use hearing protection; and an alternative if a particular activity is not accessible. Where there is a disability, accessibility rules for goods and services reinforce the duty to provide accessible information and reasonable and proportionate measures.

A short message works better than explaining an entire medical history: ‘I need to know whether there will be strobe lighting, loud sound or long queues, and whether it is possible to enter and leave during the activity.’

title: Physical activity, sport and swimming
lede: Physical activity can mean walking, dancing, swimming, cycling, training, playing or moving in whatever way is possible for the person. There is no single sport ‘for neurodivergent people’: what matters is that the activity is accessible, safe and chosen.

p: A small group if needed; clear instructions; visual demonstration; the same structure from one session to the next; a visit beforehand; breaks; adjustments to noise, changing facilities or physical contact; and the option of an individual activity if the team format creates a barrier.

Ask about quiet lanes or time slots, water temperature, swimming-cap rules, hairdryer noise and changing-room rules. For some people, the hardest part is not swimming but entering the changing room, waiting, showering or getting out of the water.

Where there is a disability, accessibility and non-discrimination also apply to goods, services and sporting activities open to the public. This does not guarantee every imaginable adjustment, but it does require reasonable and proportionate measures to be considered.

title: Leisure, art, music, animals and nature
lede: Leisure does not need to be therapeutic. It can be rest, an interest, creativity, movement or connection with other people.

p: Offer activities because the person enjoys them, not because they ‘work on skills’. An intense interest can be a route to belonging and learning without having to become a career.
Flexible duration, queue-free entry where that option exists, headphones, advance information, space to step away, a companion and the option to take part only in part of the activity.

Distinguish between living with animals, animal-assisted activities and assistance dogs. A companion animal may support wellbeing, but that does not give it the access rights reserved for accredited assistance dogs.

title: Assistance dogs: what the law recognises
lede: Real Decreto 409/2025 establishes a national framework for the work and welfare of assistance dogs and recognises several categories, including dogs for autistic people. Specific recognition and accreditation are also coordinated with regional legislation.

p: The Royal Decree regulates basic requirements, training, identification, welfare and access to the environment. Assistance-dog status is not obtained simply by buying or independently training a companion dog: there is a formal process, and organisations or professionals involved must meet specific requirements.

Define the specific tasks the dog is expected to perform, who will take responsibility for daily care, costs, waiting times, living arrangements, travel and what will happen as the dog grows older. For children, the family plays a central role in handling and welfare.

The national framework protects access for the assistance-dog partnership to many spaces and services, without prejudice to regional details. It is advisable to check the accreditation required in the autonomous community where the person lives.
